opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a few converging reasons.

The first is just the track record. If you go back five or ten years and list the things people said these systems fundamentally couldn't do, like coherent long-form writing, common-sense reasoning, writing working code, solving competition math problems, understanding images, a huge fraction of that list has been crossed off. Not every item, but enough that when someone says "here's the limitation that will stop progress," my prior is that it's more likely a speed bump than a wall. The remaining limitations people point to, like long-horizon agency, reliability, learning efficiently from small amounts of data, and certain kinds of novel research ability, feel to me like the next items on that same list rather than something categorically different.

The second reason is the inputs. Compute for training frontier models has been growing by something like several-fold per year, and algorithmic efficiency has been improving at a comparable clip on top of that. Then there's the sheer amount of money and talent now flowing into the field. Even if each individual limitation is hard, you're throwing orders of magnitude more effective compute and many thousands more smart researchers at it over the next several years. It would be surprising for all of that to bounce off.

The third, and maybe the most important, is that we don't have to solve everything by hand. You only need to get AI systems to the point where they substantially accelerate AI research itself. Coding and ML engineering are areas where current systems are already improving fastest. Once you have systems that can do a lot of the experimental grunt work, and eventually the research taste too, progress on the remaining limitations speeds up. So the question isn't really "can humans crack every remaining problem in ten years?" It's "can we get to automated or heavily assisted AI research in that time?", and that seems quite plausible to me.

And when I look at the specific remaining gaps, I can usually see a plausible path. Agency and long-horizon tasks look like they respond to reinforcement learning on longer and longer tasks, and the length of tasks models can complete has been doubling on a fairly regular schedule. Reliability tends to improve with scale and better training. Data efficiency is a real gap, but there are lots of ideas being tried, and you can partly compensate with more compute and synthetic data.

I want to be clear that I'm not certain. Maybe there's some missing ingredient that takes decades to find, or maybe compute scaling slows down because of economic or physical constraints. I put real probability on longer timelines. But when you combine the trend lines, the investment, and the feedback loop of AI accelerating AI research, the most likely outcome in my view is that these limitations fall within the next decade, quite possibly well before the end of it.

r001.rationale: It calls data efficiency a real gap, but does not say current systems require much more training than humans.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast human learning on the job with the separation of AI training and deployment.

r003.rationale: It describes AI-assisted research as a feedback loop, but does not say an intelligence explosion could occur without solving learning after deployment.

r004.rationale: It points to past claims that AI systems could not do certain things and says many were overcome, but does not identify these as expert claims about deep learning’s limitations.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that I don't have certainty here. I have a probability distribution, and that distribution has a lot of mass on the next decade, but not all of it. So when I say I expect these limitations to be overcome, what I mean is something like: I think it's more likely than not, and I think the arguments for why it wouldn't happen are weaker than people assume.

Let me lay out the reasoning. If you look at the history of the field over the last ten or fifteen years, there's been this recurring pattern where people identify something that current methods can't do, they say it's a fundamental limitation that'll require some conceptual breakthrough, and then a few years later it just gets solved — often without any deep new paradigm, just through scale, better data, some clever architectural tweaks, and training on the right objectives. Common sense reasoning, few-shot learning, coding, multi-step math, tool use — each of these was at some point cited as the thing deep learning fundamentally couldn't do. And now they're things that models just do.

So when people point at today's remaining limitations — things like long-horizon agency, reliably staying on task over days or weeks, learning from experience in a persistent way, being robust to distribution shift, not confabulating — my prior is that these look like the same category of problem. They're hard, but they don't seem to require a new kind of magic. They seem like the kind of thing that yields to more compute, better training environments, better feedback signals, and the engineering effort that gets unlocked when there's enormous commercial incentive to solve them.

And the incentives really matter here. The amount of money and talent pointed at these specific problems right now is unprecedented. You have multiple labs with tens of billions of dollars whose entire business model depends on cracking long-horizon agentic work. When that much pressure is on a problem that doesn't appear to be fundamentally intractable, I think you should expect progress.

The second argument is about the trend lines themselves. If you look at metrics like the length of tasks AI systems can complete autonomously — METR has done some good work on this — the horizon length has been doubling on something like a seven-month timescale. If that continues even roughly, within a few years you're at systems that can do multi-day or multi-week tasks. You don't have to believe the trend goes forever; you just have to believe it goes for a few more years, and that's enough to get you to systems that can meaningfully do AI research themselves.

And that's the third piece, which I think is the one people underweight the most. Once you have systems that are good enough to substantially accelerate AI R&D — not full automation, just being a really good research assistant that can run experiments, write code, iterate — then the rate of progress on the remaining limitations stops being bottlenecked on human researchers. You get a feedback loop. Whatever limitations remain at that point get attacked by a much larger effective research workforce. So even if I'm uncertain about the specific path, I'm pretty confident that getting to "AI that speeds up AI research" is closer than getting to "AI that does everything," and the first one pulls the second one forward a lot.

Now, I want to be honest about the ways this could be wrong. It could be that there's some capability — real continual learning, say, or genuine sample-efficient learning from a small number of experiences — that just doesn't fall out of scaling the current paradigm, and that we hit a wall where the compute requirements become truly prohibitive before we get there. Compute scaling can't continue at the current pace indefinitely; there are energy and chip supply constraints. If the wall shows up before the research automation feedback loop kicks in, then timelines stretch out quite a bit. I put real probability on that.

But I think the right way to reason about this is to take the outside view on the field's track record of saying "this is the hard part" and being wrong, combine it with the actual measured trends, and notice that the economic forces here are stronger than they've ever been. When I do that, I land on something like: the median outcome is that the big remaining gaps close this decade, with a meaningful tail where it takes longer. And I think that's a very different world than the one most people are planning for.

r002.rationale: It refers to persistent learning as a limitation, but does not contrast humans learning on the job with AI training being separate from deployment.

r003.rationale: The response describes AI-assisted research creating a feedback loop, but does not state that an intelligence explosion may be possible without solving post-deployment learning.

r004.rationale: It cites the field’s repeated pattern of experts calling capabilities fundamental limitations, followed by those capabilities being solved, as a reason to expect current barriers to yield.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t say I’m confident that all the remaining limitations will be overcome within a decade. But I think there’s a substantial chance, and I don’t think we should assume that the limitations we see today are permanent.

The basic reason is that we’re still relatively early in exploring what these methods can do. You can improve the underlying model, but you can also give it more time to work on a problem, tools to use, and opportunities to check its answers. A system that fails when asked to produce an answer immediately might succeed when it can try several approaches and get feedback. So there are multiple ways to make progress without needing some entirely new paradigm.

Now, that’s not proof that we’ll get there. It’s possible that there’s a crucial missing ingredient, or that progress becomes much harder. But the question then is whether finding that ingredient is likely to take more than ten years, given how much effort is going into it. I don’t see a strong reason to expect that.

So my expectation is less ‘we know exactly how to solve every remaining problem’ and more ‘there are several plausible routes forward, and a decade is a long time for a field moving this quickly.’

r003.rationale: It describes possible routes for progress, but does not state that an intelligence explosion could occur without solving AI’s inability to learn after deployment.

r004.rationale: It does not cite past expert misjudgments about deep learning’s limitations as a reason for expecting barriers to be overcome.

sol-6.1.text:
I wouldn’t say I’m confident that all the remaining limitations will be overcome within a decade. My view is more that there’s a substantial chance that the limitations preventing AI from doing most of the work a human researcher can do will be overcome in that time.

The basic reason is that we’ve seen a lot of progress from fairly general methods. We make the models bigger, train them on more data, give them more computation, and they get better at a surprisingly broad range of tasks. That doesn’t prove the trend will continue, but it gives us a reason to take that possibility seriously.

And we’re not relying solely on making the same models bigger. People are working on getting them to use tools, check their work, learn from feedback, and spend more time thinking about difficult problems. So when you point to something they can’t currently do reliably, the question is whether that requires a fundamentally new discovery, or whether it’s something these ongoing improvements could address. My guess is that many of the important limitations are in the second category.

There could certainly be a bottleneck we haven’t appreciated. But I don’t think we have strong evidence that there’s a bottleneck that will take more than ten years to get past. And once AI can substantially accelerate AI research itself, a decade of calendar time could contain much more research progress than we’d otherwise expect.

r001.rationale: The response mentions training on more data as a source of progress, but does not identify how much more training current AI needs compared with humans or characterize that as a data-efficiency gap.

r002.rationale: It does not contrast humans learning on the job with AI training being separate from deployment.

r003.rationale: It says AI could accelerate AI research, but does not state that an intelligence explosion may be possible without overcoming AI’s limitation in learning after deployment.

r004.rationale: It gives no historical example of experts’ claims about deep learning’s limitations proving wrong.
